rationale: The authorized article landing page exposes a preclinical antipsychotic review abstract. Europe PMC returned no article body, the official PDF route returned an interstitial and the matched cloud file was unavailable.

The original systematically reviews drooling definitions and prevalence in Parkinson research. Figures and symptom categories describe included studies, with no raw-fig exposure or dietary comparison.
The clinical series measures salivary-gland morphology and drooling in eight cerebral palsy patients after a prescription procedure. There is no fig consumption or Parkinson comparison.
The study measures drooling counts after a salivary procedure in 17 children with neurologic disorders. The before-and-after observations provide neither a raw-fig exposure nor a Parkinson outcome.
The prospective study compares administration groups in 21 patients with non-Parkinson brain lesions. It tracks drooling after a prescription intervention, with no food arm.
The clinical study measures drooling in tetraplegic patients after brain injury and a prescribed salivary intervention. Swallowing and posture are assessment factors and no raw fig was studied.
The review covers salivary disorders, medication effects and clinical management. Oral-cue and dietary suggestions do not contain a tested raw-fig comparison.
The review surveys medication-associated salivary dysfunction and subjective symptoms. It catalogs drug comparisons and provides no oral fig exposure.
The cadaver study evaluates localization using a dye marker. It does not measure live participant drooling or test a dietary exposure.
The systematic review summarizes six primary rimabotulinumtoxinB publications. The measured drooling outcomes relate to a prescription treatment, with no fig comparison.

The original case describes myasthenia and a medullary infarct with increased drooling and swallowing difficulty. The assessment concerns diagnostic and medical interventions without raw fig exposure.
The Wilson disease series relates drooling to oromandibular dystonia and reports multi-component medical management. The observed association is outside the Parkinson raw-fig comparison.
The therapeutic review discusses salivary physiology, symptom instruments and prescription procedures. The tabulated trials do not test raw fig intake.
The short clinical series concerns physician-administered treatment and patient-reported saliva effects. There is no fig exposure or isolated Parkinson dietary comparison.
The cross-sectional adult study measures salivary-gland localization by ultrasound and surface landmarks. Its endpoint is localization rather than a fig-related clinical symptom response.

The original review describes gastrointestinal mechanisms and dysphagia, sialorrhea and other symptoms in Parkinson disease. Its clinical, dietary and treatment passages contain no raw-fig drooling estimate.
The 132-person retrospective study compares recorded incident sialorrhea in stimulation and medically treated groups. It did not assign a dietary fig exposure.
The placebo-controlled crossover concerns prescription treatment for clozapine-associated hypersalivation in schizophrenia. It supplies no Parkinson raw-fig comparison.

The original panel article reuses the voluntary 382-response patient and caregiver survey and discusses clinical care recommendations. No fig-specific assignment or outcome is documented. Figure 1A has a separate formatting correction.
The corrigendum restores six percentage labels in the previously published survey figure. The same respondents and categories underlie both assets. It contributes no new dietary intervention.
The study computationally screens a bovine milk-derived peptide. It reports no saliva or drooling endpoint in a treated organism and no fig exposure.

The original open-label registry-linked study reports separate salivary-flow and drooling measures in 187 adults with mixed underlying conditions. The intervention is a prescription treatment, with no assigned food.
The plasma metabolite study uses drooling presence as a binary classification feature in a cross-sectional sample. Figure and biomarker results supply no raw-fig intake or severity change comparison.
The full review describes pharmacological developments for Parkinson motor and nonmotor symptoms. Its figures and recommendations address drug treatment and provide no raw-fig comparison.
